newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: S.Korea petrochemical firms consider output cuts.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea petrochemical firms consider output cuts.

text.p: South Korean petrochemical companies are considering cutting production rates at their naphtha crackers due to high naphtha prices, industry sources said on Thursday.

As a result of an extraordinary meeting in Seoul on Wednesday with one Japanese petrochemical company to discuss current high prices of the feedstock, South Korean petrochemical firms are to "seriously consider" cutting operation rates, the sources said.
"We cannot find any margin," complained one.

Naphtha prices on Asia's benchmark open-specification forward contract have hovered at post Gulf-War highs since mid-November. First-half February was talked at $241.50/$244.00 per tonne at midday on Thursday.
But the sources said no firm plan had been decided on yet.
"It is very difficult to reduce the running rate," said one petrochemical trader. "We need to meet fixed quotas."

South Korea's production of petrochemical products, including synthetic resins, fibres and rubbers, is estimated at 10.09 million tonnes this year, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said on Wednesday.
Japanese, European and South Korean petrochemical firms usually meet twice a year.

But the third meeting was called as a direct result of the decision of the seven South Korean petrochemical companies last week to suspend trade up to April arrival cargoes with Japanese trader Itochu Corp amid public allegations of price manipulation.
Itochu has declined comment on the allegations, first made by the seven South Korean petrochemical companies in a statement last week.
"Although some of the petrochemicals said it (the suspension) was not a fair decision, business will stop with Itochu," a source said.

South Korean naphtha demand is set to slump because of high international prices. Imports in February are due to drop to around four cargoes compared to the normal of up to 12 cargoes as petrochemical firms instead seek term cargoes from domestic refiners.
Domestic supplies were ample as three refiners, similarly hit by weak profit margins, have shut down reformers which use naphtha as a basic feedstock, the sources said.
